brief: Fed chair Warsh faces a hike-vs-hold dilemma this week, with markets pricing a 90% chance of a hike. Tchir argues a hike would help the long end of the curve but raise the government's interest cost by about $15 billion a year via $6 trillion of T-bills maturing in 2026, plus another $15 billion via the Fed's $6.7 trillion balance sheet, mostly funded overnight. He argues hiking would not fix inflation's real driver, supply-constrained oil and diesel, and would not slow AI compute spending, which depends on addressable-market perception rather than rates; he would therefore hold. Separately, Bessent is making his own job harder by mocking "Bloomberg Bros" publicly; absent more forceful action (monetizing gold, pushing Fed QE) or a lighter investment-grade issuance calendar, Tchir sees 10-year yields reaching 5% over time, though he is mildly, tactically bullish the long end. A strike has shut the pipeline Saudi Arabia uses to bypass the Strait of Hormuz; diesel sits at a record high on tight refining capacity and Ukrainian strikes on Russia, while the strategic reserve has drawn to 285 million barrels.
